book.title: The Telegraph All New Cryptic Crosswords 4

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father
a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: A priest who happens to be on good terms with the Pope.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma tempts you to read 'Father' as a priest and the definition; the definition is the phrase at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Papal is the adjective for anything belonging to or issued by the head of the Roman Catholic Church.

indicators.note: in a down answer, going up means the word is read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: screw is prison slang for a warder

explanation.surface: Someone who has botched a job and has to begin over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screw up' reads as one phrasal verb meaning blunder; split it, and screw is the jailer while up is the direction signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To redraw is to draw something again from the beginning, so to start the drawing afresh.

clue.text: Rant about Arab leader for column

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for rant goes around the other piece

parts.note: to bluster is to talk loudly and aggressively, to rant

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter of Arab is used

parts.note: only the opening letter of this word is wanted

explanation.surface: A tirade about some Arab ruler written up as a newspaper column.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Column' suggests journalism, but it is the architectural sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A baluster is a short pillar, one of the small columns that support a stair rail or balustrade.

clue.text: Head of police with finish imminent

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, so only the first letter of police is used

parts.note: only the opening letter of this word is wanted
an ending is a finish

explanation.surface: A chief constable whose retirement is about to happen.
explanation.definitionFit: Something pending is about to happen or awaiting decision, so it is close at hand.

indicators.note: the security word is placed around the royal abbreviation

parts.note: defence is protection, so security

explanation.surface: Royal protection officers guarding the monarch out of respect.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, for Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword shorthand for the Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Deference is courteous regard and submission to another's wishes, a form of respect.

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, so the letters of the two words are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: the nine letters of these two words are the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An actor playing King Lear gives such a bad performance that he gets hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a wounded actor; the nine letters of the first two words simply rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacerated means cut or torn, so wounded or hurt, physically or in feelings.

indicators.note: without its top means the first letter of the chest word is lost

parts.note: a coffer is a strongbox or chest for valuables

explanation.surface: An instruction to bare one's chest, as at a topless beach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' suggests nudity, but it only removes the first letter of a word for chest.
explanation.definitionFit: To offer something, such as resistance or a view, is to present or show it.

parts.note: f, for forte, is the musical direction meaning loud
an earful is a long scolding

explanation.surface: A shouted reprimand that is truly dreadful to hear.
explanation.definitionFit: Fearful can mean very bad or dreadful, as in a fearful mess, the same sense as appalling.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ... out, the past tense of spit
second meaning: a petty quarrel or squabble

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a bouncer throwing someone out of a brawl; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Spat is the past tense of spit, expelling something from the mouth, and also a noun for a minor quarrel.

indicators.note: smashed means broken into pieces, so these letters are reassembled differently

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wrecked and smashed after taking a drug, both words meaning heavily intoxicated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrecked' and 'smashed' both look like slang for drunk or high; one is the definition and the other the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship that has run aground is stranded on the shore or a reef, which is how it is wrecked.

parts.note: plane as an adjective means flat or level, so even

explanation.surface: A question about whether Earth has a uniform temperature.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: Earth is one planet among several.
explanation.definitionFit: Earth is an example of a planet, a world orbiting the Sun.

clue.text: Idiot Tory with idiotic tendency initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of each of the four words is used

parts.note: the opening letters of these four words are taken in order

explanation.surface: A jibe at a foolish Conservative politician given to idiocy.
explanation.walkthrough: Tory is the everyday name for a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A twit is a British informal word for a silly or foolish person.

clue.text: Cautioned, if on diet, to change

indicators.note: the letters of the three words are told to change, that is to rearrange themselves

parts.note: the eight letters of these three words are the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A patient warned that, if dieting, they must change their habits.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is taken loosely: to caution someone is to give them formal notice or warning.
explanation.definitionFit: To be notified is to be informed or formally warned of something, close to being cautioned.

clue.text: Tape of band taking Ecstasy line

indicators.note: taking means holding inside, so the two pieces sit within the band word

parts.note: a ring is a circular band
a cord is a length of line or string

explanation.surface: A cassette of a rock group taking drugs and snorting a line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' and 'line' play on music and drugs; band is a ring and line is a cord. E is the slang abbreviation for the drug Ecstasy.
explanation.definitionFit: A tape is a recording, a performance captured on magnetic tape.

clue.text: Terrible drivel by Yankee creating mischief

indicators.note: something terrible is a mess, so the letters of drivel are put in a new order

parts.note: the six letters of this word are the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An American talking dreadful nonsense and stirring up trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Devilry is wild, wicked behaviour, mischief worthy of a devil.

clue.text: Suspicion of sepia by sea creature

parts.note: sepia is the brown ink of the cuttlefish
a ling is a long sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: A hint that a squid's brown ink is close to some marine animal.
explanation.definitionFit: An inkling is a slight suspicion or vague hint of something.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to gather together, a verb
second meaning: a brief set prayer read in church on a given day

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass' looks like the church service, which sits well beside a prayer; here it is the verb to gather.
explanation.definitionFit: To collect is to gather in a group, and a collect is a short liturgical prayer of the Western Church.

indicators.note: new letters are made from the old, so the three words are rearranged

parts.note: the eight letters of these three words are the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone is rude to a recent arrival in the country.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose but fair: a newcomer to a country starts as someone from outside.
explanation.definitionFit: An outsider is a person not belonging to a group or community, as a newcomer from abroad is at first.

clue.text: With bottle opener, drunk journalist turned red

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter, so only the start of bottle is used

parts.note: only the opening letter of this word is wanted
a lush is a heavy drinker, a drunk
ED is short for editor, the senior journalist

explanation.surface: A tipsy reporter with a bottle opener, his face going red.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottle opener' reads as the tool; it means the first letter of bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: To blush is to go red in the face from embarrassment, so blushed means turned red.

clue.text: Martini for example, putting bird on back!

indicators.note: the bird word goes on, that is before, the word for back

parts.note: a cock is a male bird
the tail is the back end of an animal or thing

explanation.surface: Mixing a Martini with a parrot perched on your back.
explanation.definitionFit: A Martini is a classic mixed drink of gin and vermouth, an example of a cocktail.

parts.note: taken as written
a den is a private room for study or work

explanation.surface: A port wine discovered in someone's study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' suggests the drink kept in a study; it is the seaport in Yemen.
explanation.definitionFit: Aden is a major seaport on the Gulf of Aden in Yemen.

parts.note: minute as an adjective means tiny; wee is Scottish for small

explanation.surface: A remark that time is precious, perhaps just a minute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minute' reads as a unit of time beside 'time'; it is the adjective meaning tiny.
explanation.definitionFit: Precious and twee both describe something affectedly dainty or overly quaint.

clue.text: Former wife soundly criticised, getting stretch

parts.note: an ex is a former spouse

indicators.note: soundly here means going by how the word is heard, not how it is written

parts.note: to pan a show is to criticise it harshly

explanation.surface: An ex-wife thoroughly criticised and then sent to prison for a stretch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soundly' looks like it means thoroughly, but it signals that panned is taken by its sound.
explanation.definitionFit: To expand is to grow larger or extend, which is to stretch.

indicators.note: gripping means holding, so the fever word clasps the letter for right

parts.note: ague is an old word for a malarial fever with shivering

explanation.surface: A debate gripped by excitement over what is right.
explanation.definitionFit: To argue is to put forward reasons for or against, which is to debate.

parts.note: a commercial is an advertisement, an ad
vice is wickedness or evil

explanation.surface: A television commercial carrying a warning about wickedness.
explanation.definitionFit: Advice can be a caution or recommendation about what to avoid, which is a kind of warning.

indicators.note: chasing means running just behind; here the letter leads straight into the fish word
the head of a word is its opening letter, so only the first letter of ship is used

parts.note: only the opening letter of this word is wanted
a kipper is a smoked herring

explanation.surface: A trawler's captain out hunting a shoal.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a fishing boat's master spends his days chasing fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A skipper is the captain of a ship, especially of a fishing boat, so it is the vessel's head.

parts.note: nags are old or worn-out horses

explanation.surface: Jumps set up for a pony race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hurdles' suggests horse jumps, but it means obstacles; S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small.
explanation.definitionFit: Snags are unexpected obstacles or difficulties, which is what hurdles are figuratively.

clue.text: English leader dismal in stern manner

indicators.note: the first letter and the word for dismal sit in the middle of the word for stern

parts.note: dour means stern and severe in manner

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the opening letter of English is used

parts.note: only the opening letter of this word is wanted
mean can mean shabby and wretched, so dismal

explanation.surface: An English captain whose mood is gloomy, presented in a strict way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stern manner' reads as one phrase, but 'stern' is part of the wordplay and 'manner' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Demeanour is a person's outward behaviour or bearing, the way they carry themselves.
